Loi 21 à la Cour suprême : débat sur la: Bill 21 at the Supreme Court: a debate over the notwithstanding clause, while on the ground, lives and careers have already been upended.

Pour la réalisation de ce reportage, je: For this report, I travelled to Ottawa with a colleague to attend the first day of hearings at the Supreme Court of Canada, which must decide whether or not the legal rules were correctly applied in the case of Quebec’s Bill 21 on secularism.
Des entretiens ont été menés sur place a: Interviews were conducted on site with demonstrators who say they have been harmed by Bill 21, as well as with lawyers involved in the case. Other sources, including legal experts, were consulted afterward to put the issues in context and explain how the Supreme Court and the current process work.
<strong>À Ottawa, devant et à l’intérieu: In Ottawa, in front of and inside the Supreme Court of Canada, the first day of hearings on Bill 21 saw two realities intersect: the concrete one of women and families who say their careers have been held back or cut short, and the more abstract one of a legal debate over the limits of the notwithstanding clause. Between hope for change and uncertainty, the Court is being asked to rule on an unprecedented question whose repercussions could redefine the balance between fundamental rights and legislative power in Canada.
Devant le bâtiment de la Cour suprême du: In front of the Supreme Court of Canada building, more than a hundred people gathered at dawn on Monday, March 23, 2026. Some hold signs, others talk in low voices. Many are simply waiting. The group is made up mostly of Muslim women who wear the hijab, joined by members of the Sikh community, recognizable by their dastar, and many travelled from Quebec cities, notably Québec City and Montréal.
Ces communautés sont les plus touchées p: These communities are the most affected by<l1> Bill 21</l1>, adopted in June 2019, which bans the wearing of religious symbols by Quebec government employees in positions of authority, such as judges, police officers, Crown prosecutors, school principals and teachers. Quebec used the<l2> notwithstanding clause (section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms)</l2> to shield Bill 21 from court challenges.
Celles et ceux qui ont fait le déplaceme: Those who made the trip on Monday did not come to attend the hearings. They came to tell their stories. Leila, 44, stands slightly apart. She watches the comings and goings in front of the building while keeping an eye on her children. She arrived in Canada in 2022, and this mother of three had hoped to continue a teaching career after working in the field for over a decade in her country of origin. “I was told I was excellent, but that I had to take off my scarf,” she says. “I refused. It’s part of me.” Since then, she says, she has given up on several job opportunities. “It’s not just economic. It’s depressing. I love teaching.”
Comme Leila, plusieurs femmes rencontrée: Like Leila, several women we met describe careers held back or cut short because of Bill 21, or of Bill 94, which aims to strengthen secularism in Quebec’s school system, notably by banning staff from wearing religious symbols.
Karima Benzaïd, éducatrice à Laval depui: Karima Benzaïd, an early childhood educator in Laval for more than 25 years, describes an abrupt halt. “Bill 94 ended my career overnight,” she says. And the consequences go beyond work. “Today, I depend entirely on my husband. I have debts. It turned my life upside down,” she confides.
À quelques mètres de là, Brahim, venu ac: A few metres away, Brahim, who came with his wife Leila, watches the crowd. For him, the law’s impact extends beyond the current generation. “My daughter wants to become a lawyer. But she wonders whether she’ll be able to practise in Quebec,” he explains. “With every decision she makes, she asks herself, ‘Is this going to be possible with this law?’”
Dans certaines familles, l’idée de quitt: In some families, the idea of leaving the province is taking shape. “We’re thinking about moving to Ontario,” he adds. “To give our children a better future.”
En haut des escaliers de la Cour, l’accè: At the top of the Court’s steps, access is screened by discreet police officers and a security team that manages the flow according to the building’s capacity. Cases heard by the Supreme Court don’t usually draw such a large crowd, let alone so many parties. This time, the Court will hear 51 applicants, among the challengers alone. This first day is reserved for groups that are challenging the law, including the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA), the English Montreal School Board (EMSB), the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), and the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement du Québec (FAE).
Dans le vestibule, des rangées de chaise: In the lobby, rows of chairs have been set up for the public. Silence is observed. Phones go quiet. All eyes are fixed on the two screens broadcasting the hearing. At 9:30 a.m., the arguments begin.
Dans la grande salle d’audience de la Co: In the Supreme Court of Canada’s main courtroom, the atmosphere is solemn, almost suspended. On the bench,<l1> seven judges take their seats</l1>. Two are missing: Mahmud Jamal, who chose to recuse himself to avoid any controversy over his supposed opposition to Bill 21 because of his past involvement with the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (a request had in fact been filed in 2024 by the Mouvement laïque québécois (MLQ) to remove him from the Bill 21 case, claiming he would not be impartial); and Mary T. Moreau, absent with no public explanation. It is also worth noting that, of the nine judges, three are from Quebec.
Le ton est calme, posé. Mais derrière ce: The tone is calm and measured. But behind this composure, the rigour is palpable. The judges, led by Chief Justice Richard Wagner, intervene frequently, interrupting the lawyers to ask for clarification, test a hypothesis, push a line of reasoning to its limits. The exchanges are dense, technical, at times abrupt, but never break with the restraint that defines the place.
Les avocats doivent immédiatement s’ajus: The lawyers have to adjust immediately, rephrase, add nuance, defend every word. The debate takes the form of a demanding exchange, where the magistrates’ quiet confidence contrasts with the parties’ constant effort to persuade.
<strong>« Reformuler l’utilisation de la: “Reformulate the use of the notwithstanding clause”
Parmi les organisations entendues figure: Among the organizations heard is the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement (FAE). Met as he left the hearing, its lawyer, Frédéric Bérard, says the issue goes far beyond Bill 21.
« On demande à la Cour de reformuler le: “We’re asking the Court to reformulate the text governing the use of the notwithstanding clause, because today it’s too easy to suspend fundamental rights,” he explains. Concretely, the FAE is asking the Court to set a precedent, he continues, and to “add a substantive condition to limit how easily legislators can override fundamental rights.”
Selon M<sup>e</sup> Bérard, la perte d’e: According to M<sup>e</sup> Bérard, losing a job over wearing religious symbols is a serious violation of protected freedoms. “Losing a job simply for exercising a freedom protected by the charters is appalling,” he says.
Pour comprendre ce qui se joue dans cett: To understand what is at stake in this room, we need to go back to the Supreme Court’s particular role. “It’s the highest court in the country. It doesn’t rehear the facts. It checks whether the legal rule was correctly applied,” explains Dallal Boukhari, a doctor of law and the author of a thesis titled <l1>Étude de la compatibilité de la laïcité française au Québec à partir de la « Charte des valeurs québécoises »</l1>.
Contrairement aux tribunaux inférieurs,: Unlike lower courts, the Court chooses the cases it hears. It considers legal questions of national importance. In the case of Bill 21, adopted in 2019, the court path is already long. Challenged as soon as it came into force, the law was examined by Quebec courts following legal action brought notably by teachers who wear the hijab and by groups such as the Ligue des droits et libertés. In April 2021, the Quebec Superior Court recognized that the law infringed fundamental rights but upheld its application because the notwithstanding clause had been invoked, a decision confirmed on appeal by the Quebec Court of Appeal in October 2022, despite reservations about the scope of the clause.
Cette clause permet à un gouvernement pr: This clause allows a provincial government to temporarily exempt a law from certain protections in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, for a renewable period of five years.
C’est précisément cette utilisation qui: It is precisely this use that is now being challenged. “The Court will not directly rule on the validity of Bill 21,” Dallal Boukhari explains. “It will examine the use of the notwithstanding clause itself, particularly its preventive use.”
Autrement dit : un gouvernement peut-il: In other words: can a government invoke this clause as soon as a law is adopted to prevent any challenge on the merits? “This is a first,” the legal scholar points out. “The Supreme Court has never ruled on this question.”
Dans la salle, les arguments se succèden: In the courtroom, the arguments follow one after another. Lawyers for the groups challenging the law stress its concrete effects, notably on linguistic and religious groups. Lawyers representing the Jewish community also make their case on this first day before M<sup>e</sup> Wagner and his colleagues.
Avant même l’ouverture des plaidoiries à: Even before arguments opened at the Supreme Court of Canada, the tone had already been set. Outside the courthouse, as in the public sphere, voices in favour of Bill 21 reacted, framing the debate from the outset as a political power struggle. On its digital platforms, the Parti québécois called the hearings a “trial of Quebec,” arguing that the challenges aim to “undermine Quebec’s right to legislate on [its] model of living together.” The party defends the notwithstanding clause as “the only legislative tool” that can protect Quebec’s distinctiveness.
À l’intérieur de la Cour, cette position: Inside the Court, this position translates into legal arguments. Speaking on the second day, the representative of Quebec’s attorney general, M<sup>e</sup> Isabelle Brunet, argued that the notwithstanding clause is a democratic choice and that “it is not the Court’s role to decide a political question.”
À la sortie de la Cour, en fin de journé: At the end of the day, outside the Court, the group gathered again. Some had followed the hearings from inside, others had waited outside. Conversations resume, sometimes animated, sometimes quiet. Leila is still there. “I hope someone will understand that you can’t build a country by limiting freedoms,” she says simply.
Autour d’elle, les attentes sont à la fo: Around her, expectations are both high and cautious. Everyone knows the decision won’t come right away.
Après les quatre jours d’audience, les j: After the four days of hearings, the judges will withdraw to deliberate. The ruling could take several months. That said, the Supreme Court of Canada generally issues its opinion before the end of summer. But for those who were there that day, what mattered most has already happened elsewhere: in being there, in bearing witness, in seeing their reality, for once, carried all the way to the country’s highest judges.
Ce qui se joue à Ottawa dépasse les murs: What is at stake in Ottawa goes beyond the Court’s walls. The institution could uphold Bill 21 as is, or strike it down in whole or in part, or issue a nuanced decision, limiting its application in certain specific cases or redefining how the notwithstanding clause may be used in the future. The judges would then have to determine whether banning religious symbols for teachers and the other positions concerned constitutes discrimination.
Une telle décision créerait un précédent: Such a decision would set a precedent across the country. But for Leila, Karima or Brahim, these scenarios remain abstract. What they live with is very real: a job refused, a career interrupted, a future plan called into question.
Sur le parvis de la Cour suprême du Cana: On the forecourt of the Supreme Court of Canada, people turn to look at the building one last time before everyone heads home. Behind those walls, judges and lawyers continue their exchanges, in the calm and rigour of the law.
